title: RAW UNREVIEWED: one shifted centre jointly changes endpoint distances and burden while the span persists
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. Complete cached Vitruvius X.3.7–9 links equal carrying shares, a slipped burden strap, a yoke adjusted to help a weaker ox, and the common shorter-side/heavier-burden relation. One written centre argument jointly determines both endpoint distances; the same span persists. The later helping prescription must put the weaker participant on the longer side. This is actual configuration change, not a passive observer or unit conversion. No exact torque law or target meaning is assigned.

design.role: One bounded independent pipeline producer; root owns selection and authorship
design.whole_content: A practical explanation begins with equal burden at the centre of carrying poles and precautions against strap slipping. It then describes shifting a yoke attachment to help a weaker ox, explains how the same moved centre makes one side shorter and the other longer, and applies the common distance/burden comparison to carrying and draught. The conclusion situates these examples within the source's rectilinear-axis/circular-motion account. Repeated relational grammar can carry the geometry and comparison without a different stage dictionary for each example.

source.work: Vitruvius De architectura, entire X.3.7–9; complete X.3.1–9 read as context
source.edition: Morgan1914 English translation of the ancient work; cached Project Gutenberg20239. No medieval native witness, Latin collation or new acquisition.
source.complete_unit: Three entire paragraphs7–9, not one isolated inverse-distance phrase. Four/six porters, centre nails, strap slip, the steelyard analogy, unequal ox strength, shifted yoke attachment, unequal described circles and the concluding list of machines remain content obligations if this whole unit is claimed.
source.paragraph7: Heavy loads are carried on poles by four or six porters. Central attachment distributes an equal share; nails mark the centres to prevent slipping. A shift beyond the centre burdens the nearer place more heavily, compared with a steelyard weight moving from equilibrium.
source.paragraph8: Middle attachment gives equal draught; unequal ox strength motivates shifting the strap so that a longer side helps the weaker ox. Moving the attachment away from the middle shortens one side and lengthens the other. Rotating the ends around that attachment describes larger and smaller circles respectively.
source.paragraph9: The author compares wheels, then explicitly says shorter centre-to-end intervals bear harder on the neck and longer intervals ease draught/carriage. The chapter concludes by placing these and listed machines under its straight-axis/circular-revolution account.
source.context_limit: Paragraphs1–6 include hoisting, lever reversal, steelyard, steering, sail height and oars. They were read but are not silently required target clauses of7–9. The sail-speed and wheel claims are historical assertions, not modern controlled mechanical findings. No claimed modern physical adequacy or numerical force equation follows.

shared_written_obligations.reference: For each described pole/yoke, the centre/attachment C is one argument shared by both endpoint-distance expressions. Endpoint identities A and B persist within that example. Carrying and draught examples remain separate objects; one common grammar does not make them the same physical beam or people.
shared_written_obligations.invariant: Under the explicitly paid straight fixed-span interpretation, A and B delimit an unchanged positive span L and C lies between them. DIST(A,C)+DIST(C,B)=L before and after the attachment shifts. The source explicitly describes one side shortening as the other lengthens; the additive length identity is an analytical representation of that geometry, not a source-written equation or bound numeral.
shared_written_obligations.comparison: Use the same distance relation and common C for both sides. The author's qualitative burden rule says a shorter centre-to-end side bears harder and a longer one eases burden. No absolute threshold of shortness, participant-specific lexical value or freely selected comparison standard substitutes for the shared centre.
shared_written_obligations.scope: Participant strength/ability and imposed burden are separate properties. An equal central share does not assert equal ox strength. Four or six porters are not silently reduced to two people: A/B can denote endpoint-side aggregates only with that aggregation explicitly paid, and the source's full porter grouping remains owed.
shared_written_obligations.physical_change: The attachment actually moves on the apparatus. A passive change of coordinate origin without moving it cannot produce a newly redistributed burden. This candidate concerns an altered geometrical reference point with physical role; it does not supply IDEA849's unit conversion or identify an observer-frame operator.

linked_consequences.steps: Bind one span and its two endpoints; bind an interior attachment shift toward A; evaluate both endpoint distances from the same new attachment; apply the author's shorter/longer burden rule.
linked_consequences.consequence: The A-side distance shortens and B-side lengthens. A bears the harder burden and B the easier burden in this declared historical account. Independent endpoint descriptions that both lengthen, or two different unexpressed centres, cannot keep the paid fixed span and common reference. No numeric load or exact reciprocal force law follows.
linked_consequences.research_decision: A whole C0 composition that reuses the shared reference in the two distance expressions and a later burden comparison has a concrete cross-clause obligation. If each side receives an independent stage label, retain RAW but do not call it productive relational composition.

linked_consequences.steps: Bind the weaker/stronger ox relation without changing their identity; consume the common distance/burden rule in the later purpose of helping the weaker ox.
linked_consequences.consequence: The weaker ox must be on the longer, burden-easing side; the shifted attachment is therefore nearer the stronger endpoint under the paid fixed-span model. Moving it toward the weaker endpoint instead produces the source's harder-burden side there. This derives a direction from a prior relation and stated purpose, without a new directional gloss for each stage.
linked_consequences.research_decision: A frozen whole reading assigning the weaker participant to the shorter side cannot satisfy this specific content account merely by renaming help or weakness. Reject that fixed relation assignment; do not repair it by silently swapping participants.

linked_consequences.steps: Reuse the common attachment in the source's circular-end comparison after establishing the unequal distances.
linked_consequences.consequence: The farther endpoint is the endpoint of the larger described circle, and it is also the burden-easing side under the common rule. An independent circle-size list cannot attach larger to the nearer endpoint while preserving the same centre and distances. Different rotation angles/paths must be explicit if introduced; no new source drawing or observed revolution is asserted.
linked_consequences.research_decision: An actual written later circle comparison can consume the earlier distance relation. Its absence in a claimed whole7–9 account is a content omission, not permission to pad the remaining native groups.

counterexamples_and_rivals.name: passive coordinate rebasing
counterexamples_and_rivals.difference: Changing written coordinates of an unmoved strap does not redistribute the real burden. It can preserve geometric descriptions, but cannot supply the source's attachment-change consequence without an actual configuration argument.

counterexamples_and_rivals.name: intrinsic participant burden
counterexamples_and_rivals.difference: Assign harder burden only from strength or identity. It cannot explain the pole's slip case with unchanged participants, or the common shorter-side rule, without a separate spatial/configuration relation.

counterexamples_and_rivals.name: two independently chosen local centres
counterexamples_and_rivals.difference: Each endpoint receives its own free short/long standard. It removes the joint span and complementary-distance obligations rather than expresses the offered account.

counterexamples_and_rivals.name: compiled configuration recipe
counterexamples_and_rivals.survival: A named middle/offset configuration directly returns a pair of endpoint loads and circle descriptions. It can preserve all these source facts without a productive relational operator. A source-only account cannot exclude it.

counterexamples_and_rivals.name: generic allocation with an internal divider
counterexamples_and_rivals.survival: Jointly rename beam/span/attachment/distance/burden into a fixed budget, divider, shares and inverse costs. This preserves the declared qualitative geometry and obligations. It prevents unique mechanical meaning selection; it does not prevent exploratory whole C0 authorship.

counterexamples_and_rivals.name: modern exact statics
counterexamples_and_rivals.limit: An exact torque or support-reaction equation requires added assumptions about straight rigid beams, forces, beam weight, contact and loading. It is not silently imported as source-grounded truth, a numeral prediction or a test gate.
